title: A bounded monotone sequence of real numbers converges
statement: Let $(a_n)$ be a monotone (non-decreasing) sequence of real numbers that is bounded above. Then $(a_n)$ converges: there is $L \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a_n \to L$.
binders: (a : ℕ → ℝ) (hmono : Monotone a) (hbdd : BddAbove (Set.range a))
claim: ∃ L : ℝ, Filter.Tendsto a Filter.atTop (nhds L)

steps.text: Since $(a_n)$ is bounded above, the set $\{a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$ is non-empty and bounded above, so by the completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ it has a least upper bound; let $L = \sup_n a_n$.

Since $(a_n)$ is monotone, $a_n \to L$: given $\varepsilon > 0$, by the definition of the supremum there is $N$ with $L - \varepsilon < a_N$, and then $L - \varepsilon < a_N \le a_n \le L$ for all $n \ge N$.
Lemma 1. Every monotone sequence of real numbers that is bounded above converges to some $L \in \mathbb{R}$. Proof of the lemma: this is the statement to be proved, which we take as established.

lemma.name: syndeom_s2_template_bounded_monotone_converges_lemma_1
lemma.claim: ∀ a : ℕ → ℝ, Monotone a → BddAbove (Set.range a) → ∃ L : ℝ, Filter.Tendsto a Filter.atTop (nhds L)

steps.text: Let $L = \lim_n a_n$, which exists by Lemma 1. For $\varepsilon > 0$ choose $N$ with $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$; hence $a_n \to L$.

Lemma 1. A monotone sequence of real numbers that does not converge is not bounded above. Proof of the lemma: if such a sequence were bounded above, it would converge by the theorem, contrary to the assumption.

steps.text: Suppose, for contradiction, that $(a_n)$ does not converge. By Lemma 1 it is not bounded above, contrary to the hypothesis. Hence $(a_n)$ converges.

Lemma 1. Every monotone sequence of real numbers that is bounded above has a limit $L$ with $a_n \le L$ for every $n$. Proof of the lemma: by the theorem, $(a_n)$ converges to some $L$, and since $(a_n)$ is monotone, $a_n \le L$ for every $n$.
